generalfeedback.text:
For each pair work out \(y \div x\) and \(x \times y\). If \(y \div x\) is the same every time, it is direct proportion; if \(x \times y\) is the same every time, it is inverse proportion; if neither stays the same, it is neither.

Table 1: \(y \div x\): \({@jn(rt[1])@}\); \(x \times y\): \({@jn(pr[1])@}\). [[if test="is(kd[1]=1)"]]The ratio stays the same, so \(y = {@rt[1][1]@}x\): directly proportional.[[elif test="is(kd[1]=2)"]]The product stays the same, so \(xy = {@pr[1][1]@}\): inversely proportional.[[elif test="is(kd[1]=3)"]]Neither stays the same: \(y\) rises with \(x\), but there is a starting amount, so \(y\) is not \(0\) when \(x\) is \(0\). Neither.[[else]]Neither stays the same: \(y\) falls as \(x\) rises, but falling is not enough for inverse proportion. Neither.[[/if]]

Table 2: \(y \div x\): \({@jn(rt[2])@}\); \(x \times y\): \({@jn(pr[2])@}\). [[if test="is(kd[2]=1)"]]The ratio stays the same, so \(y = {@rt[2][1]@}x\): directly proportional.[[elif test="is(kd[2]=2)"]]The product stays the same, so \(xy = {@pr[2][1]@}\): inversely proportional.[[elif test="is(kd[2]=3)"]]Neither stays the same: \(y\) rises with \(x\), but there is a starting amount, so \(y\) is not \(0\) when \(x\) is \(0\). Neither.[[else]]Neither stays the same: \(y\) falls as \(x\) rises, but falling is not enough for inverse proportion. Neither.[[/if]]

Table 3: \(y \div x\): \({@jn(rt[3])@}\); \(x \times y\): \({@jn(pr[3])@}\). [[if test="is(kd[3]=1)"]]The ratio stays the same, so \(y = {@rt[3][1]@}x\): directly proportional.[[elif test="is(kd[3]=2)"]]The product stays the same, so \(xy = {@pr[3][1]@}\): inversely proportional.[[elif test="is(kd[3]=3)"]]Neither stays the same: \(y\) rises with \(x\), but there is a starting amount, so \(y\) is not \(0\) when \(x\) is \(0\). Neither.[[else]]Neither stays the same: \(y\) falls as \(x\) rises, but falling is not enough for inverse proportion. Neither.[[/if]]

questiondescription.text:
Compound Proportions: direct, inverse or neither

Grade 12 CBE Core 1.3 / Essential 1.2 (b): Decide from a table whether one quantity is directly proportional, inversely proportional, or neither, to another.

Core and Essential

This question is adapted from Chapter 7 (Direct and inverse proportion), Section F, question F3 of Ling, J., Scruton, P., Shilton, S. and West, H., SMP GCSE Mathematics: Higher 2 for AQA, Edexcel and OCR two-tier GCSE mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 2007: new Kenyan contexts and tables, with two named traps (a fixed starting amount, a fall that is not inverse) and options in a dropdown.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core and Essential Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text:
[[if test="is(ans1=1)"]]

[[if test="is(kd[1]=3)"]]\(y\) rises as \(x\) rises, but rising is not enough for direct proportion: [[else]]For direct proportion, [[/if]]\(y \div x\) must be the same for every pair. Here \(y \div x\) is \({@jn(rt[1])@}\). Check \(x \times y\) as well before you decide.

[[elif test="is(ans1=2)"]]

[[if test="is(kd[1]=4)"]]\(y\) falls as \(x\) rises, but falling is not enough for inverse proportion: [[else]]For inverse proportion, [[/if]]\(x \times y\) must be the same for every pair. Here \(x \times y\) is \({@jn(pr[1])@}\). Check \(y \div x\) as well before you decide.

[[else]]

Neither means that \(y \div x\) changes from pair to pair and \(x \times y\) changes too. Work out both for every pair in this table: one of them stays the same.

[[/if]]
